brief.entity: Spencer Alexander Lawyers is a Box Hill, Melbourne law firm acting for parents and grandparents in parenting plans, consent orders and court proceedings about children, with the principal overseeing every matter.
bullets: A court making a parenting order treats the child's best interests as the paramount consideration, and there is no presumption of equal shared parental responsibility.
Each parent has parental responsibility for a child under 18, and separation alone does not change that.
An application for parenting orders generally needs a family dispute resolution certificate, unless the court grants an exemption.

sections.h2: When families call us about the children.
paras: Most people call soon after separating, when the children are moving between two homes on an arrangement nobody has written down, or one parent wants a pattern the other will not accept. Others have agreed and want it recorded, have orders that no longer fit, or face a move that would make it much harder for the children to see a parent.

Many people still call these arrangements custody. The law now speaks of parenting orders, which can set out who a child lives with, the time the child spends with other people and who is responsible for making decisions about the child.
We act for mothers and fathers, and for grandparents and others concerned with a child's care, who can apply for parenting orders themselves.

sections.h2: What we do in parenting matters.

items.p: We draft parenting plans, which are written agreements between the parents about where the children live, their time with each parent, holidays and decisions. A plan must be signed and dated, and made free of any threat, duress or coercion. It cannot be enforced as orders can, but a court making orders has regard to the latest plan where that is in the children's best interests.

Once you agree, we prepare the application and the proposed orders. In the application, each of you tells the court of any concern about abuse, family violence or risk. Consent orders have the same force as orders made after a hearing.
We advise whether you need a certificate or can ask the court for an exemption, prepare you for mediation, and turn any agreement into terms precise enough to work.

Where agreement is not possible, we apply for or respond to interim and final parenting orders, changes to final orders, recovery orders and orders to stop a child being taken out of Australia. If you are in immediate danger, call 000.

sections.h2: What to have with you when you call.
paras: Whatever you have to hand: any parenting plan or court orders, any intervention order, letters from the other parent or their lawyer, a note of the current arrangements, and your questions. If you have little on paper, that is fine too. The first conversation is about understanding your situation, not testing your paperwork.
Our office is at Suite 10, 1 Main Street, Box Hill, a short walk from Box Hill station, with parking at Box Hill Central.

process.h2: How a parenting matter moves forward.

steps.d: Where it is safe, you try family dispute resolution first, since an application needs the practitioner's certificate or an exemption from the court.
An agreement is recorded in a parenting plan or filed as an application for consent orders, which the court can make, seek more information about, or dismiss.

Otherwise the application is filed with the certificate or an exemption request and the Notice of Child Abuse, Family Violence or Risk that every parenting application needs, and the court decides, treating the children's best interests as paramount.

fee.p: Our fixed fee for consent orders for agreed parenting arrangements is $3,025 including GST. faqs.q: Do the children have to spend equal time with each of us?
faqs.a: No. The Family Law Act does not start from equal time or any other split, and since May 2024 there has been no presumption of equal shared parental responsibility. The court weighs the matters the Act lists for the particular child, starting with the safety of the child and their carers, and equal time remains possible where it is in the child's best interests.

faqs.q: Do we have to try mediation before going to court?
faqs.a: Usually. Unless the court grants an exemption, an application for parenting orders needs a family dispute resolution certificate, which a practitioner can also give if the other parent refuses or fails to attend. Exemptions are available for urgent applications and applications made by consent, among others. The court can also grant one where it is satisfied there are reasonable grounds to believe that a party has committed family violence or abused the child, that there is a risk of family violence by a party, or that the child would be at risk of abuse if the application were delayed. If you are in immediate danger, call 000.

faqs.q: Is there a time limit for parenting orders?
faqs.a: The Family Law Act sets no deadline, but no parenting order can be made for a child who is 18 or over, is or has been married, or is in a de facto relationship. Before filing, the court's rules expect you, where it is safe, to try family dispute resolution and, if that fails, to give written notice of the orders you will seek, with a genuine offer and at least 14 days to reply.

faqs.q: Can I move away with the children?
faqs.a: You should not, without the other parent's agreement or a court order, if the move would make it significantly harder for the children to spend time with that parent. The Act treats that as a major long-term issue. Where it is safe, parents are encouraged to consult each other about it, and where a parenting order provides for joint decision-making, they must consult and genuinely try to decide together. Moving first and asking later can seriously damage your case.

faqs.q: What if the other parent is keeping the children from me?
faqs.a: If you are in immediate danger, call 000. Otherwise call us the day it happens. The court can order a child's return to a parent, deal with a breach of existing orders, and excuse family dispute resolution where an application is urgent.
